analysis.one_liner: Orders the futures regulator to use emergency powers to curb excessive speculation in energy markets.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the Senate Agriculture Committee and died there without a hearing, a vote, or a single cosponsor.
analysis.plain_summary: In the summer of 2008, gasoline was over $4 a gallon and crude oil had just hit a record $139 a barrel. Senator Maria Cantwell's bill would have directed the Commodity Futures Trading Commission, the agency that oversees energy futures trading, to use every tool it had, including its emergency powers, to curb excessive speculation that was pushing energy prices beyond what supply and demand could explain. The bill never got a hearing or a vote in the committee it was sent to.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary consumers paying gasoline, diesel, and heating oil prices, along with airlines, truckers, and farmers whose fuel costs had roughly doubled or tripled since 2001, if curbing speculation actually lowered prices. The Commodity Futures Trading Commission would also gain a clear mandate from Congress to act.

how_it_helps.text: Directs the CFTC to use all its authority, including emergency powers, to immediately curb excessive speculation in energy futures and swaps markets [S2] [S3].
Targets price distortion and 'unwarranted changes in prices' that prevent energy markets from accurately reflecting supply and demand [S2] [S3].
Responded to record energy costs: crude hit $139.12 a barrel in June 2008, regular gasoline averaged $4.07 a gallon, and diesel $4.77, roughly double or triple 2001 levels [S3].
Cited the IMF's May 2008 finding that it was 'hard to explain current oil prices in terms of fundamentals alone,' suggesting speculation played a significant role [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Traders, hedge funds, and index funds holding large speculative positions in energy futures would face position limits or other curbs, reducing their ability to profit from rising energy prices. Futures exchanges would face pressure to enforce those limits on their markets.

drawbacks.text: Many economists argued that oil's rise was driven by fundamentals, mainly growing demand from China and other Asian nations, not speculation; the bill's own findings acknowledge rising demand during the decade [S3].

If speculation was not the main cause of high prices, emergency intervention could have disrupted hedging markets that airlines, truckers, and oil producers use to manage legitimate risk, without lowering prices at the pump.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: If the speculation theory was right, the bill offered a fast, no-new-spending way to take speculation out of energy prices that families and businesses were paying. If the theory was wrong, the cost was mainly reduced liquidity in futures markets. The honest uncertainty was that the causes of the 2008 price spike were genuinely disputed among economists.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to the Senate Agriculture Committee on the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before Congress ended in January 2009.

narrative.text: Senator Cantwell introduced the bill on June 26, 2008, at the height of the oil price spike [S1] [S3].
It was read twice and referred to the Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry the same day [S1] [S5].
No further action was taken; the bill had zero cosponsors [S4] [S5].
Congress ended on January 3, 2009, and all bills not passed die when a Congress ends [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Traders and funds holding speculative positions in energy futures were better off, since no curb on speculation was enacted. The CFTC also kept full discretion over whether and how to use its emergency powers, rather than being directed by Congress to act.

for.name: Maria Cantwell
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill; it had no cosponsors

against.name: Senate Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry
against.role: Senate committee with jurisdiction over commodity futures regulation
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and never scheduled a hearing or vote on it

sides.party_line_note: There was never a vote or recorded opposition, and the bill had no cosponsors of either party, so no partisan pattern is visible in the record.

industries.industry: Energy futures speculators (hedge funds, index funds, large traders)
industries.note: The bill would have ordered the CFTC to curb excessive speculative positions in energy futures and swaps, which the bill's findings tied to record oil, gasoline, and diesel prices paid by consumers and businesses. Their profit opportunity from rising energy prices would have been curtailed.
Exchanges where energy futures trade would have faced immediate emergency action and enforcement on their contract markets, though the bill imposed no new structural limits on exchange business.

These industries would have benefited from any reduction in fuel prices; the bill's findings note airlines were forecast to spend $20 billion more on jet fuel in 2008 than 2007, and truckers and farmers were paying diesel near $4.77 a gallon.
